author: mdalandete-alt
body:
## The problem

`/weekly`, `/monthly` and `/sunday-review` all read `journal-index.json`. **Nothing rebuilds it when a journal is written** — there is no hook and no scheduled task.

The insights skills guard the index with a staleness check:

> If the index doesn't exist or is more than 7 days old, rebuild it first

That check measures **age, not completeness**. A one-day-old index passes it while still missing every entry written since it was built.

## What this looked like in practice

In one vault the index sat at **21 indexed entries against 26 on disk**, and the vault went **seven weeks without generating a single weekly or monthly report**. Nothing surfaced the failure: the index was never "old", just incomplete, so the guard never fired and the reports silently had nothing to work from.

## The fix

The index is *derived* from the journals, so it should be refreshed when one is **written**, not when someone remembers to check.

- **`skills/daily-journal/SKILL.md`** — adds the rebuild to the top of Step 9 (after saving), with the expected output and an explicit instruction not to continue silently if it fails. Notes that `--vault-root` / `--journal-dir` are required for localized or emoji-prefixed folder names, and that Windows needs `python`, not `/usr/bin/python3`.
- **`skills/insights/SKILL.md`** — one line so the 7-day guard is not mistaken for a completeness check, and points at the write-time rebuild as the first thing to check when entries are missing.

Docs only — no script or behavior changes.

body:
## What

Three ideas were considered for extending MineClone:
1. **Pressure plates / mechanisms** — the world reacting to weight (chosen)
2. Jukebox with procedural music — a new "listen" verb, but ambience without gameplay depth
3. Sunken shipwreck with loot — duplicates the "stumble upon" verb just introduced by mineshafts (#80)

Pressure plates won because until now literally everything in the game happened only on a direct player click — the *mechanisms* dimension didn't exist at all. New verb: **automate**.

## Feature

- **Pressure plate** — new Tab-menu item: a wooden plate entity (like rails, not a voxel) placed with RMB on solid ground. Any weight on top — player, mobs, animals, minecarts — depresses the lid with a click and activates it; when the weight leaves (small delay), it clicks off. LMB removes it; it pops off if its support is mined or its cell is filled.
- **Automatic doors** — a pressed plate opens adjacent closed doors and gates (radius 1 horizontally, ±1 vertically) and holds them; on release it closes only what it opened itself (hand-opened doors are untouched), politely: it won't close through a creature standing in the doorway and won't fight another pressed plate holding the same door.
- **TNT trap** — pressing ignites TNT in the 3×3×3 cube around the plate (including under it) with a short fuse: plate by the wall + hidden charge = mobs blow themselves up.
- **Two new achievements** — «⚙ Механік» (place a plate) and «🪤 Пастка!» (a mob steps on your plate); 97 total, counted by the meta-achievement.
- **Persistence** — plates are saved with the world; old saves stay compatible.
- Zero external assets: model, icon and click sounds are procedural. Debug helpers: `MCDebug.givePlate()`, `placePlateAt()`, `placeDoorAt()`, `placeGateAt()`, `plateInfo`.

## QA

Headless Playwright run against the real game: 12/12 checks pass (plate placement, press by player, door auto-open/auto-close, release after stepping off, popping without support, TNT ignition, achievement unlock, no console errors).

## Summary

This branch records the project's versioning strategy as an accepted
Architecture Decision Record (ADR) and adopts retrievable episode TEI
revision history as a planned capability. It answers two questions raised
during the 4.3.2 alpha review: whether the home-rolled versioning approach
was ever recorded as a decision (it was not), and whether any roadmap task
covered retrievable episode TEI history (none did).

ADR-018 is retrospective: it consolidates decisions taken piecemeal across
ExecPlan decision logs, migrations, and earlier ADR fragments into one
record of the shared strategy — explicit repository-written history in one
unit of work, compare-and-set versus insert-once-then-reuse as two named
concurrency shapes, content-addressed immutability, audit-protecting
deletion policy, and version pinning at consumption boundaries — including
why ORM-level versioning libraries such as `sqlalchemy-continuum` are not
used. ADR-019 then extends the established history-table pattern to episode
TEI, and roadmap step 2.8 carries the two implementing tasks.

Roadmap task: (2.8), added by this branch.

author: depo-dev
body:
Closes #1057
Closes #1035

**All work in this PR targets the `dev` branch. This PR must not be merged directly into `main`.**

## Summary

Removes the Soroban operator key from the API process, puts a validating policy in front of every signature, makes signing haltable without a redeploy, adds envelope encryption so master-key rotation becomes a rewrap rather than a migration, and clears the gosec backlog behind #1035.

Before this change `stellar.ContractInvoker` parsed `STELLAR_OPERATOR_SECRET` into a `keypair.Full` and held it for the process lifetime (`invoker.go:36`), applying it unconditionally at three call sites. Code execution in the API therefore yielded **the key itself**, not merely the ability to request a signature — and nothing evaluated *what* was being signed.

## Security Architecture

```
API container                          signer container
  builds + simulates                     authenticate caller
  (no key needed)                        check kill switch
        │                                validate intent
   RemoteSigner ──── unix socket ────▶   apply policy
                     0660, or mTLS       check replay
   holds: DB creds, JWT secret,          rebuild + sign
          cipher keys                    ────────────────
   holds NOT: operator key               holds: operator key
                                         holds NOT: DB creds
```

**A separate signer process was chosen over a KMS deliberately.** A KMS gives strictly stronger custody — the key would be non-extractable even from the signer host — but this deployment (`docker-compose.yml`: plain containers, no cloud IAM, no workload identity) has no way to authenticate to one. Adding a stub or "local KMS" would be exactly the fake security control the issue prohibits. `signing.Backend` is the seam: a real KMS implementation can replace `stellar.SigningBackend` without touching the policy, audit, or kill-switch layers.

Two further properties worth noting:

- **The signer cannot broadcast.** It returns a signed envelope; submission stays with the API, so a compromised signer cannot quietly push transactions without the API observing them.
- **The signer has no database credentials.** A deliberate trade, discussed under Risks.

## Threat Model

`docs/security/signing-threat-model.md` enumerates every secret the API loads with storage, process access, what compromise permits, blast radius, rotation, revocation, and — the field usually left vague — **whether compromise is actually detectable**.

Two entries deliberately say it is not:

- **`AUTH_JWT_SECRET`** — a forged token is cryptographically indistinguishable from a real one; it verifies against the same secret. Detection depends on behavioural session telemetry that does not exist. **Current detection latency: unbounded.**
- **Account cipher keys** — offline decryption by anyone holding the key and a database copy produces no application-observable event.

Recording that plainly is more useful than implying controls that are not there.

## Signing Isolation

The boundary carries a **typed transaction intent, never raw bytes**. A `Sign(raw []byte)` primitive would make the signer a general oracle and reduce the value of moving the key to almost nothing. Instead the caller describes the operation and **the signer rebuilds the transaction itself** — a signature can only ever cover a transaction the signer constructed from an intent it approved.

The authorized set is closed at eight operations, mirroring the eight call sites in `soroban_vault_chain_invoker.go`: `pause`, `unpause`, `rebalance`, `emergency_withdraw_all`, `deposit`, `withdraw`, `harvest`, `set_weights`.

**Caller authorization** is Unix socket permissions (the kernel refuses unauthorized callers before any application code runs; world-writable modes rejected at startup) or mutual TLS with `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` pinned on and a CA pool that starts *empty* rather than from system roots. `SIGNER_SHARED_SECRET` was rejected on purpose: a secret in the API's environment authenticates "whoever holds the API's environment" — precisely the attacker the boundary exists to contain.

**Latency budget: < 5 ms boundary overhead. Measured: 28.6 µs/op** over 200 iterations — ~175× headroom. End-to-end signing remains dominated by the Soroban RPC round trip for simulation (100–2000 ms), which this does not affect.

## Encryption / Key Rotation

`crypto.EnvelopeCipher` implements the standard envelope pattern with stdlib AES-256-GCM. No cryptography is invented and no dependency is added.

- Fresh data key per record — one compromised data key exposes only its own record, and nonce reuse across records cannot arise.
- The key version is authenticated as AAD when wrapping, so an altered stored version fails to unwrap rather than being tried against the wrong master key.
- Optional AAD binds a ciphertext to its row, so one moved between rows fails authentication instead of decrypting into the wrong record.
- Any configured version unwraps; only the active version wraps. That asymmetry is what makes mid-rotation reads work.
- A failed authentication tag is an error. **No fallback to another key, none to plaintext.**

`rotation.RewrapRotator` is idempotent, resumable, commits per row, and **re-counts pending rows before reporting success** — claiming success while rows remain is the precondition for retiring a key those rows still need. `VerifyRetirable` makes that check explicit before a key leaves the configuration.

## Audit Integrity

Every signing outcome — **including every rejection** — produces an audit event carrying intent ID, caller, operation, contract, key ID, an intent hash, outcome, rejection category, and latency. It carries no key material, no signed envelope, no authorization headers.

The existing hash-chained `internal/audit` service is reused rather than duplicated, per the issue's instruction not to introduce a second architecture.

**On what tamper-evidence actually provides:** the chain detects modification, deletion, and reordering. An attacker with `DATABASE_DSN` write access who *recomputes the chain forward* produces something internally consistent — only external anchoring catches that. Documented explicitly rather than claiming immutability.

## Kill Switch

A sentinel file at `SIGNER_KILL_SWITCH_PATH`. Its presence halts signing.

```bash
docker compose exec signer touch /var/run/nester-signer/signing.disabled
```

Requires host- or orchestrator-level access to the signer, not an application credential — the authority to halt signing must not be obtainable by compromising the application you are halting. It works when the database is down, when Redis is down, and when the API is fully compromised.

**Fail-closed.** Three states: `enabled`, `disabled`, and `unknown` (sentinel unreadable — permission denied, I/O error, broken mount). **`unknown` blocks signing.** Being unable to confirm signing is permitted is not permission to proceed. A signer with no configured switch path refuses to start.

## Incident Response

`docs/security/incident-response.md` — written for the on-call engineer at 3am who did not write this code. Literal commands, not "investigate the issue".

Covers detection (with the honest statement that signals are recorded but **not alerted**, so latency is "whenever someone looks"), containment, evidence preservation *before* restarts, blast-radius assessment, rotation, recovery, and communication.

The highest-value investigative step is §C.3: **reconcile on-chain operator activity against the audit stream.** Chain activity with no matching audit event means the key was used *outside* the signer — exfiltration, not merely API compromise, and it changes the response.

body: ## Summary - ⌘⇧0 (Equalize Pane Splits) and the pane context-menu item of the same name were no-ops in v2 workspaces: the store recomputed every split percentage, but the panels never moved. - `SplitView` now pushes the store's split percentage into the `ResizablePanelGroup` through its imperative handle whenever the percentage changes. ## Why / Context `react-resizable-panels` treats `defaultSize` as mount-time-only — after mount, panel sizes live in the group's own layout state and only change via a drag or `setLayout`. `equalizeTab`/`equalizeSplit` rewrite `splitPercentage` in the panes store, which re-rendered `ResizablePanel` with a new `defaultSize` that the library ignores. The v1 workspace uses react-mosaic (fully controlled), which is why only v2 was affected. Same root cause for both entry points, since both call `equalizeTab` on the store. ## How It Works An effect keyed on the node's split percentage compares the group's current layout to the store's value and calls `setLayout([first, second])` when they differ (0.01 tolerance). `setLayout` is a no-op when the layout already matches, and it re-emits `onLayout`, so any value the library clamps is written back to the store — no feedback loop, and dragging still owns the layout while the user is dragging. The sync is general, not equalize-specific: any store-driven size change (e.g. a preset layout) now reaches the DOM. ## Manual QA Drove the running dev app over CDP (v2 workspace, real key/mouse input), measuring `data-panel-size` plus screenshots before and after: - **Repro before the fix**: ⌘T, ⌘D, ⌘⇧D, dragged the root divider to 26.5/73.5, pressed ⌘⇧0 → sizes unchanged (26.5/73.5). - **After the fix**, same journey → 33.3/66.7 (leaf-weighted equal areas), divider visibly moves. - Equalize pressed twice in a row is stable (no jitter). - Oscillating drags across the handle with mid-gesture dwells and an induced 120ms/400ms main-thread stall: no feedback loop, `console.error` empty. - Dragging after an equalize still works (33.3/66.7 → 17.1/82.9), so the sync effect doesn't fight the user. - Three-level nesting: [6.3/93.7, 38.1/61.9, 50/50] → [25/75, 33.3/66.7, 50/50]. - Context-menu "Equalize Pane Splits": [5.1/94.9, …] → [25/75, …]. - Layout survives leaving the workspace route and coming back, so store and DOM agree. ## Testing - `bunx turbo test --filter=@superset/panes` — 100 pass - `bunx turbo test --filter=@superset/desktop` — 2792 pass - `bunx turbo typecheck --filter=@superset/panes --filter=@superset/desktop` - `biome check` on the changed file https://claude.ai/code/session_01Td2NUVeMANb1qfap6xtzxt --- ## Summary by cubic Equalizes pane splits in v2 workspaces by pushing store-driven sizes into the `ResizablePanelGroup` layout. Previously, ⌘⇧0 and the “Equalize Pane Splits” menu were no-ops; now panes move to the equalized sizes and any store-driven size change applies. - Adds a `useEffect` in `SplitView` that reads the group layout and calls `setLayout([firstSize, secondSize])` when it differs (0.01 tolerance). - Maintains drag behavior: `setLayout` is a no-op when matching and re-emits `onLayout`, so clamped values flow back to the store without feedback loops. - Scope: v2 (`react-resizable-panels`) only; v1 (`react-mosaic`) was already controlled and unaffected. Written for commit d88d7c965d857074ed5577b2b3183b1f687094bb. Summary will update on new commits. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Bug Fixes** * Improved split-panel layout synchronization when split sizes change. * Prevented unnecessary layout updates when the current arrangement is already within the expected tolerance. * Added safeguards for unavailable split groups or unexpected panel configurations.
